A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites and videos so they can be delivered quickly, no matter where a visitor happens to be. Normally, every request for a page or video travels to one main computer, called the origin server, which holds the original, official copy of everything. If that origin server is far away, loading feels slow. To fix this, copies of popular content get placed on nearby computers called edge locations, positioned closer to where people actually are. When a request arrives and the nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer comes back almost instantly without bothering the distant origin server at all. If no copy exists yet, the edge location fetches it once from the origin, saves it, and future requests become cache hits. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books in stock, so people don't have to travel to the one national archive every time they want to read something common. This setup reduces waiting time, prevents overload on the origin server, and keeps things working smoothly even when many people request the same content simultaneously. The result is faster loading, fewer errors, and a more reliable experience for everyone browsing online, especially during busy periods.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer holding the true, master copy of a website's content | It's the ultimate source, but relying on it alone for everyone makes things slow |
| Edge location | A nearby computer storing a copy of popular content | It shortens the distance content has to travel, speeding up delivery |
| Cache hit | When requested content is already saved at an edge location | It means near-instant delivery without contacting the origin server |
| Cache miss | When requested content is not yet saved nearby and must be fetched first | It explains why a first request can be slower than later ones |
